title: Measurements of $Z$-boson pair entanglement in decays of Higgs bosons at the ATLAS experiment
comment: 36 pages in total, author list starting page 19, 6 figures, 1 table, published in PRL. All the figures and tables are available at https://atlas.web.cern.ch/Atlas/GROUPS/PHYSICS/PAPERS/HIGP-2024-25/
summary: Entanglement is a key property of quantum systems. In this Letter the first measurements of quantum entanglement between spins in pairs of $Z$ bosons are reported, using proton-proton collision data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at center-of-mass energies of 13 TeV and 13.6 TeV, recorded with the ATLAS detector. Measurements of angular observables sensitive to $ZZ^*$ spin-density-matrix elements in the $H\rightarrow ZZ^* \rightarrow \ell^+\ell^-\ell^+\ell^-$ process yield coefficients $C_{2,1,2,-1} = -0.71 \pm 0.45$ and $C_{2,2,2,-2}=0.08 \pm 0.44$, consistent with their Standard Model predictions. A complementary hypothesis test using the full angular distribution, and relying on several Standard Model assumptions in the decays, provides substantially higher sensitivity to quantum correlations and disfavors the separable-state hypothesis at a significance of 4.7 standard deviations (expected $4.9σ$) relative to the entangled Standard Model hypothesis. These results provide strong evidence of quantum entanglement between massive bosons (spin qutrits) at the electroweak scale.

AI.tldr: Measurements of quantum entanglement between spins in $Z$ bosons from LHC data show strong evidence contrary to the separable-state hypothesis and align with Standard Model predictions.
AI.motivation: To investigate and confirm quantum entanglement properties of $Z$ bosons produced in high-energy proton-proton collisions.
AI.method: Analyses of angular observables related to the $Hightarrow ZZ^* ightarrow 	ext{four leptons}$ decay, calculating spin-density-matrix elements and testing against Standard Model predictions.
AI.result: Measured coefficients indicate consistency with the Standard Model, and a significant hypothesis test shows a high degree of quantum correlations with a significance of 4.7 standard deviations against separable states.
AI.conclusion: These results provide strong evidence for quantum entanglement between massive bosons at the electroweak scale.

title: Typical entanglement in anyon chains: Page curves beyond Lie group symmetries
summary: We study bipartite entanglement statistics in one-dimensional anyon chains, whose Hilbert spaces are constrained by fusion rules of unitary pre-modular categories. Our setup generalizes previous frameworks on symmetry-resolved entanglement entropy for non-abelian Lie group symmetries to the setting of quantum groups. We derive analytical expressions for the average anyonic entanglement entropy and its variance. Surprisingly, despite the constrained Hilbert space structure, the large $L$ expansion has no universal $O(\sqrt{L})$ or $O(1)$ symmetry-type corrections except for a subleading topological correction term that produces a Page curve asymmetry. We further show that the variance decays exponentially with system size, establishing the typicality. Numerical simulations of the integrable and quantum-chaotic golden chain Hamiltonian show that chaotic mid-spectrum eigenstates match the Haar-random predictions, supporting the use of eigenstate entanglement as a diagnostic of quantum chaos. Our results establish the anyonic Page curve as an appropriate chaotic benchmark in topological many-body systems and connect anyonic entanglement to Page-type universality in quantum many-body physics.

AI.tldr: This study investigates bipartite entanglement in anyon chains under unitary pre-modular categories, revealing that the average entanglement entropy behaves consistently with topological features, while also linking eigenstate entanglement to quantum chaos.
AI.motivation: To extend the understanding of bipartite entanglement statistics in anyon chains by bridging concepts from quantum groups and non-abelian symmetries, and to establish significant benchmarks in topological many-body systems.
AI.method: Analytical expressions for average entanglement entropy and variance were derived, complemented by numerical simulations of the golden chain Hamiltonian to test chaos predictions.
AI.result: Findings indicate that entanglement entropy expands without universal symmetry-type corrections, except for a topological term. The variance decays exponentially, and chaotic mid-spectrum eigenstates align with Haar-random predictions.
AI.conclusion: The study connects anyonic entanglement to the Page curve and proposes the anyonic Page curve as a benchmark for chaos in topological many-body systems.

title: Exploring LSST's capabilities for early detection of outbursts in low-mass X-ray binaries
summary: Following long periods of quiescence, low-mass X-ray binaries can exhibit intense X-ray outbursts triggered by instabilities within the accretion disk. These outbursts can sometimes be detected in optical wavelengths before being detected in X-rays, acting as an early onset warning and enabling a deep study of accretion disk properties informed by the lag between optical and X-ray rise. We explore the potential of Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) to detect these outbursts early through optical observations. We evaluate the capabilities of LSST based on currently planned survey cadence, filter-specific depth, and other observational factors that affect early detection. We develop and apply an extended metric to assess outburst detectability and recovery fraction. We find that despite inherent potential for early detection of XRB outbursts, the currently planned survey strategy makes it challenging to detect early onset of XRBs. Lastly, we demonstrate how this estimate can be used to infer the wider LMXB population in the Galaxy as the LSST progresses.

AI.tldr: The paper assesses the potential of the LSST to detect early X-ray binary outbursts through optical observations but finds current survey plans inadequate for effective early detection.
AI.motivation: Understanding X-ray outbursts in low-mass X-ray binaries (XRBs) can enhance our knowledge of accretion disk instabilities and the properties of these systems via early optical detection.
AI.method: The authors evaluate LSST's potential for early detection using planned survey cadence and filter depth, developing a metric for outburst detectability and recovery.
AI.result: The study reveals that the current LSST survey strategy presents challenges for early detection of XRB outbursts despite their inherent potential.
AI.conclusion: Results can inform the understanding of the larger LMXB population in the Galaxy as LSST continues, but improvements in survey strategies are needed for effective early detection.

title: Scalable topological quantum computing based on Sine-Cosine chain models
summary: This work proposes a scalable framework for topological quantum computing using Matryoshka-type Sine-Cosine chains. These chains support high-dimensional qudit encoding within single systems, reducing the physical resource overhead compared to conventional qubit arrays. We describe how these chains can be used in Y-junction braiding protocols for gate operations and in extended memory architectures capable of storing multiple qubits simultaneously. Fidelity analysis shows partial topological protection against disorder, suggesting this approach is a possible pathway toward low-overhead quantum hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for topological quantum computing using Sine-Cosine chains to enhance qudit encoding efficiency, demonstrating potential for reduced resource use and improved fidelity against disorder.
AI.motivation: The need for more efficient quantum computing architectures that minimize physical resource overhead while maintaining high fidelity and robustness against disorder.
AI.method: Utilizing Matryoshka-type Sine-Cosine chains for qudit encoding and Y-junction braiding protocols for effective gate operations and memory storage.
AI.result: The framework supports high-dimensional qudits and exhibits partial topological protection against disorder, indicating a promising avenue for developing low-overhead quantum hardware.
AI.conclusion: This approach represents a significant advancement in scalable quantum computing, potentially leading to more efficient hardware solutions.

title: Particle Acceleration in Cassiopeia A Revealed by Broadband High-Energy Spectrum
summary: Recently, the GeV--sub-PeV spectrum of supernova remnant (SNR) Cassiopeia A (Cas A), one of the youngest and most well-studied SNRs in our Galaxy, has been updated by observations of Fermi-LAT and LHAASO. We revisit Cas A with our previous shell-plus-jet asymmetric model and investigate its particle acceleration ability. The broadband fitting results suggest that the double-peaked gamma-ray spectrum can be well attributed to proton-proton (PP) collisions and inverse Compton scattering within the SNR shell, while the synchrotron emission from a jet component with velocity of $\sim0.1c$ can account for the hard X-ray emission up to 220 keV. Furthermore, the PP collisions in the jet can produce a sub-PeV emission, but constrained by the LHAASO-KM2A limit to a flux below $\sim 1\times10^{-14}\rm erg/(cm^2s)$ at 100 TeV. The energy of accelerated protons in the jet of Cas A could be up to $5\times10^{47}$ erg, which, assuming that the PeV cosmic ray distribution is clumpy in the Galaxy with the clump size comparable to the thickness of the Galactic plane, derives a proton flux consistent with the observed one at 1 PeV, implying that the Cas A-like SNRs can still be PeVatrons in the Galaxy. It is encouraging for LHAASO and future telescopes to detect or constrain Cas A spectrum above 100-TeV more precisely.

AI.tldr: The study revisits the particle acceleration mechanisms in supernova remnant Cassiopeia A, attributing its gamma-ray spectrum to proton collisions and inverse Compton scattering, while suggesting it has the potential to be a PeVatrons with further observations needed for confirmation.
AI.motivation: To explore the particle acceleration mechanisms in Cassiopeia A using updated observations and model analysis.
AI.method: Utilized a shell-plus-jet asymmetric model to analyze the gamma-ray and X-ray emissions from Cassiopeia A, particularly focusing on particle collisions and synchrotron emissions.
AI.result: Identified that the double-peaked gamma-ray spectrum results from proton-proton collisions and inverse Compton scattering, with hard X-ray emissions explained by a fast jet component. Estimated the proton energy in the jet could reach $5\times10^{47}$ erg, compatible with observational data.
AI.conclusion: Cassiopeia A has the potential to be a PeVatron, supporting the idea that similar SNRs could contribute to the observed PeV cosmic rays in the Galaxy, warranting future observational efforts.

title: The Gravitational-Wave Power Gap in Core-Collapse Supernovae: Insights from 60 Axisymmetric Simulations
comment: Comments are welcomed Submitted to Classical and Quantum Gravity: Focus Issue on Core Collapse Supernova Gravitational Wave Astronomy and Astrophysics: Past, Present, and Future Pages: 32, figures: 12, tables: 3
summary: We analyse the gravitational-wave emission from 60 two-dimensional core-collapse supernova simulations. The models cover a range of progenitors and equations of state. We focus on the narrow frequency interval in the gravitational-wave spectrum where the emitted power is strongly suppressed (the power gap) and how its central frequency relates to the physical properties of the simulations. We find that the power-gap frequency exhibits strong and systematic correlations with the properties of the inner core of the forming neutron star, for example the sound speed, suggesting that the gap encodes information about the behaviour of matter at extreme densities. We further examine how well several mechanisms proposed in the literature account for the presence and evolution of the gap in our simulations. Finally, we explore a scenario in which the gap arises from destructive interference between a narrow oscillation mode and a broadband background signal, demonstrating that such an interaction can produce a sharp minimum in the emitted gravitational-wave power.

AI.tldr: The study examines gravitational-wave emissions from 60 core-collapse supernova simulations, focusing on the power gap in the spectrum and its correlations with neutron star properties.
AI.motivation: Understanding gravitational-wave emissions can provide insights into the behavior of matter at extreme densities during core-collapse supernovae.
AI.method: The authors analyze simulations across varied progenitors and equations of state, specifically investigating the power gap frequency and its relation to inner core properties.
AI.result: The research establishes significant correlations between the power-gap frequency and inner core characteristics like sound speed, revealing the gap's encoded information about extreme matter behavior.
AI.conclusion: A proposed scenario involving destructive interference could explain the power gap, suggesting that gravitational-wave emissions hold vital information about the forming neutron star's internal structure.

title: Recoil geometry determines electromagnetic counterparts from supermassive black hole merger remnants
summary: Merging binary black holes embedded in gaseous environments, such as supermassive black hole binaries following gas-rich galaxy mergers, are promising sources of multi-messenger transients in the upcoming age of space-based gravitational wave detections. In case a gravitational radiation recoil is imparted to the merger remnant, subsequent interactions between the recoiled black hole and its circumbinary disk may lead to unique post-merger electromagnetic counterparts. We present the first general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations of a recoiling black hole interacting with a magnetically arrested circumbinary disk the evolution of which has been consistently tracked through the inspiral phase. We show that the post-merger accretion dynamics, depending on the recoil geometry, exhibits qualitatively disparate jet and disk behavior. For recoils perpendicular to the disk, the inner disk remains gravitationally bound and sustains relativistic jets, while in-plane recoils lead to copious shock heating and potential jet quenching for black holes directly colliding with the disk. Oblique recoils, on the other hand, produce intermittent outbursts from jet-disk interactions owing to the tilt introduced in the accretion disk. Multi-wavelength monitoring of these electromagnetic counterparts, in conjunction with the coincident gravitational wave detection, will be able to aid in characterizing the physical conditions of the merger environment.

AI.tldr: The paper presents simulations of recoiling black holes in gaseous environments, revealing diverse accretion dynamics and jet behaviors based on recoil direction, which may provide unique electromagnetic counterparts for gravitational wave detections.
AI.motivation: To explore the interactions between recoiled black holes and circumbinary disks, aiming to enhance the understanding of post-merger electromagnetic signals in the context of multi-messenger astronomy.
AI.method: The authors conducted general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations to model the behavior of a recoiling black hole within a magnetically arrested circumbinary disk, tracking its evolution from inspiral to post-merger.
AI.result: The study found that the recoil geometry significantly influences accretion dynamics: perpendicular recoils maintain relativistic jets, in-plane recoils cause heating and possible jet quenching, and oblique recoils lead to intermittent outbursts due to disk tilting.
AI.conclusion: Monitoring the resultant electromagnetic counterparts alongside gravitational waves can provide insights into the physical conditions surrounding black hole mergers.

title: Gaia Sees Blazars Move: Locating Optical Flares Using Astrometry
summary: When blazars flare, their optical position moves. We show this by combining Gaia DR3 proper motions with epoch photometry for blazars with strong optical jet emission. In 60 of 74 sources with significant proper motion, rising flux drives the centroid upstream while fading flux drives it downstream - a near-universal pattern captured by a simple two-component model of constant extended emission and a flaring region. Using this connection, we geometrically localize the optical flares to within <1 mas of the VLBI position - a few parsecs at typical blazar distances - placing them in the innermost jet or accretion disk. This purely geometric method requires no multi-wavelength correlations or model-dependent assumptions, and provides an independent spatial anchor for localizing higher-energy flares. Per-epoch astrometry from Gaia DR4 is set to tighten our constraints even further.

AI.tldr: This study reveals that blazar flares cause shifts in optical positions, identifying a consistent pattern between flux changes and these shifts, allowing for precise localization of optical flares within the blazar's jet or accretion disk.
AI.motivation: To understand the correlation between optical flares in blazars and their positional changes, enabling better localization of these events.
AI.method: Combining Gaia DR3 proper motions with epoch photometry, the study analyzes 74 blazars to establish a relationship between optical flux changes and centroid movement, utilizing a two-component model for emission.
AI.result: In 60 out of 74 blazars, a direct correlation was found where rising flux leads to upstream motion and fading flux to downstream, allowing localization of flares within <1 mas of VLBI positions.
AI.conclusion: The method provides an independent geometric framework for pinpointing optical flares in blazars, with further improvements expected from Gaia DR4 data.

title: Reconstructing Quantum Dot Charge Stability Diagrams with Diffusion Models
comment: Code available at https://gitlab.com/QMAI/papers/diffusioncsds. Data available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19252638
summary: Efficiently characterizing quantum dot (QD) devices is a critical bottleneck when scaling quantum processors based on confined spins. Measuring high-resolution charge stability diagrams (or CSDs, data maps which crucially define the occupation of QDs) is time-consuming, particularly in emerging architectures where CSDs must be acquired with remote sensors that cannot probe the charge of the relevant dots directly. In this work, we present a generative approach to accelerate acquisition by reconstructing full CSDs from sparse measurements, using a conditional diffusion model. We evaluate our approach using two experimentally motivated masking strategies: uniform grid-based sampling, and line-cut sweeps. Our lightweight architecture, trained on approximately 9,000 examples, successfully reconstructs CSDs, maintaining key physically important features such as charge transition lines, from as little as 4\% of the total measured data. We compare the approach to interpolation methods, which fail when the task involves reconstructing large unmeasured regions. Our results demonstrate that generative models can significantly reduce the characterization overhead for quantum devices, and provides a robust path towards an experimental implementation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generative approach using a conditional diffusion model to efficiently reconstruct charge stability diagrams (CSDs) from sparse measurements in quantum dot devices, greatly reducing measurement time and maintaining key features.
AI.motivation: The time-consuming nature of measuring high-resolution charge stability diagrams in quantum dot devices hampers the scalability of quantum processors.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model is employed to reconstruct full CSDs from only 4% of the total measurements, evaluated using uniform grid-based sampling and line-cut sweeps.
AI.result: The generative model successfully recovers charge transition lines and other key features from sparse data, outperforming traditional interpolation methods, especially in large unmeasured regions.
AI.conclusion: Generative approaches can significantly accelerate the characterization process for quantum devices, offering a promising avenue for experimental implementation.

title: Generating function for Hermitian and non-Hermitian models
summary: It is well known that Hermitian and non-Hermitian models exhibit distinct physics and require different theoretical tools. In this work, we propose a unified generating-function framework for both classes with generic boundary conditions and local impurities. Within this framework, any finite lattice model can be mapped to a generating function of the form G(z)=P(z)/Q(z), where Q(z) and P(z) denote the bulk recurrence relation and boundary terms or impurities, respectively. The problem of solving for eigenstates reduces to a simple criterion based on the cancellation of zeros of Q(z) and P(z). Applying this method to the Hatano-Nelson (HN) model, we show how boundary conditions and impurities determine the location of the zeros, thereby demonstrating the boundary sensitivity of non-Hermitian systems. We further investigate topological edge states in the non-Hermitian Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model and identify its topological phase transition. Inspired by generating-function techniques widely used in discrete mathematics, particularly in the study of the Fibonacci sequence, our results establish a direct connection between non-Hermitian physics and recurrence relations, providing a new perspective for analyzing non-Hermitian systems and exploring their connections with discrete mathematical structures.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a unified generating-function framework for analyzing both Hermitian and non-Hermitian models, emphasizing boundary conditions and impurities.
AI.motivation: To bridge the analytical gap between Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems, which exhibit distinct physical behaviors and require different theoretical approaches.
AI.method: Employ a generating function G(z)=P(z)/Q(z) to relate finite lattice models to bulk recurrences and boundary conditions; analyze zeros of P(z) and Q(z) to determine eigenstates.
AI.result: Demonstrated boundary sensitivity in non-Hermitian systems, explored topological edge states in the SSH model, and identified a topological phase transition.
AI.conclusion: Establish a novel connection between non-Hermitian physics and recurrence relations, providing insights into the analysis of non-Hermitian systems and their mathematical frameworks.

title: Symmetry-resolved properties of the trace distance in thermalizing SU(2) systems
summary: We study diagnostics of thermalization in quantum many-body systems with global SU(2) symmetry, where the standard eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) is generalized to its non-Abelian form. As an eigenstate-level probe, we introduce a symmetry-resolved trace distance constructed from the block structure of the reduced density matrix. This block structure separates spin-sector probabilities from configurational fluctuations within each sector, naturally leading to a decomposition into a probability trace distance and a configurational trace distance. The microcanonical average of the former is bounded by fluctuations of the corresponding spin-sector probabilities within a microcanonical energy window, whereas the latter captures finer intra-sector fluctuations. In non-Abelian thermalizing systems, these spin-sector-probability fluctuations are constrained by the non-Abelian ETH and therefore become exponentially suppressed with system size. Numerical studies of the one-dimensional \(J_1\)--\(J_2\) Heisenberg chain are consistent with this picture and suggest that, in the thermal regime, the trace distance is asymptotically dominated by the configurational trace distance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the diagnostics of thermalization in quantum many-body systems with SU(2) symmetry, introducing a new symmetry-resolved trace distance to analyze both spin-sector probabilities and configurational fluctuations.
AI.motivation: To understand how thermalization works under a non-Abelian generalization of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) in quantum many-body systems.
AI.method: The study introduces a symmetry-resolved trace distance derived from the block structure of the reduced density matrix, separating spin-sector probabilities from configurational fluctuations.
AI.result: In non-Abelian thermalizing systems, fluctuations in spin-sector probabilities follow the non-Abelian form of ETH, leading to their exponential suppression with system size. Numerical results from the 1D Heisenberg chain support this, showing the trace distance is dominated by configurational fluctuations.
AI.conclusion: In the thermal regime of non-Abelian systems, the configurational trace distance becomes the principal contributor to the trace distance, validating the importance of intra-sector fluctuations.

title: Complexity of Quadratic Bosonic Hamiltonian Simulation: $\mathsf{BQP}$-Completeness and $\mathsf{PostBQP}$-Hardness
summary: The computational complexity of simulating the dynamics of physical quantum systems is a central question at the interface of quantum physics and computer science. In this work, we address this question for the simulation of exponentially large bosonic Hamiltonians with quadratic interactions. We present two results: First, we introduce a broad class of quadratic bosonic problems for which we prove that they are $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete. Importantly, this class includes two known $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete problems as special cases: Classical oscillator networks and continuous-time quantum walks. Second, we show that extending the aforementioned class to even more general quadratic Hamiltonians results in a $\mathsf{PostBQP}$-hard problem. This reveals a sharp transition in the complexity of simulating large quantum systems on a quantum computer, as well as in the difference in complexity between their simulation on classical and quantum computers.

AI.tldr: The paper examines the computational complexity of simulating quadratic bosonic Hamiltonians, establishing significant classifications of complexity in quantum systems.
AI.motivation: To determine the complexity of simulating large physical quantum systems, particularly focusing on bosonic Hamiltonians with quadratic interactions.
AI.method: Introduces a broad class of quadratic bosonic problems, proving their $	ext{BQP}$-completeness, and further demonstrates that extending this class yields a $	ext{PostBQP}$-hard problem.
AI.result: Two significant results: 1) A broad class of quadratic bosonic problems proven to be $	ext{BQP}$-complete, including classical oscillator networks and continuous-time quantum walks. 2) Extension to more general quadratic Hamiltonians leads to a $	ext{PostBQP}$-hard problem.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight a critical transition in the complexity of simulating large quantum systems, underscoring differences between classical and quantum computational approaches.

title: An Online Approach for Entanglement Verification Using Classical Shadows
summary: Quantum measurements are slow, while classical processors are fast, yet existing hybrid protocols never exploit this asymmetry. In this work, we propose an alternative formulation of classical estimators as online algorithms that are updated incrementally upon obtaining a new sample. Classical shadows are the natural fit for this approach: designed around the principle of measuring first and asking questions later, each snapshot is a self-contained classical description that can be processed immediately and independently. As a first demonstration, we focus on mixed state entanglement verification via PT-moments, moments of the partially transposed density matrix that provide experimentally accessible sufficient conditions for entanglement. We construct two unbiased online estimators that together characterize the fundamental challenge between memory footprint and per-shot computational cost: one scales to large systems at low moment order, the other handles high moment orders at the expense of memory exponential in system size. The online estimator certifies entanglement reliably and, by exploiting all $\binom{T}{m}$ combinations of snapshots, requires fewer samples than state-of-the-art baselines, turning entanglement detection from a purely offline diagnostic into a protocol that runs concurrently with the experiment.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new approach to quantum measurements by leveraging online classical estimators, optimizing the entanglement verification process.
AI.motivation: To address the inefficiencies in existing hybrid quantum-classical protocols by exploiting the speed difference between classical processors and the slow quantum measurement processes.
AI.method: The authors propose online algorithms for classical estimators using classical shadows, which allow for immediate processing of measurement snapshots. They create two unbiased online estimators tailored for mixed state entanglement verification.
AI.result: The new estimators efficiently balance memory use and computational cost, requiring fewer samples than traditional methods while reliably certifying entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The proposed online entanglement detection method transforms the diagnostic process into a concurrent protocol, significantly improving the efficiency of quantum experiments.

title: Digital Discovery of interferometric Gravitational Wave Detectors
summary: Gravitational waves, detected a century after they were first theorized, are spacetime distortions caused by some of the most cataclysmic events in the universe, including black hole mergers and supernovae. The successful detection of these waves has been made possible by ingenious detectors designed by human experts. Beyond these successful designs, the vast space of experimental configurations remains largely unexplored, offering an exciting territory potentially rich in innovative and unconventional detection strategies. Here, we demonstrate the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to systematically explore this enormous space, revealing novel topologies for gravitational wave (GW) detectors that outperform current next-generation designs under realistic experimental constraints. Our results span a broad range of astrophysical targets, such as black hole and neutron star mergers, supernovae, and primordial GW sources. Moreover, we are able to conceptualize the initially unorthodox discovered designs, emphasizing the potential of using AI algorithms not only in discovering but also in understanding these novel topologies. We've assembled more than 50 superior solutions in a publicly available Gravitational Wave Detector Zoo which could lead to many new surprising techniques. At a bigger picture, our approach is not limited to gravitational wave detectors and can be extended to AI-driven design of experiments across diverse domains of fundamental physics.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the application of artificial intelligence to explore innovative designs for gravitational wave detectors, revealing effective configurations that exceed existing models and promoting a broader future use of AI in experimental physics.
AI.motivation: To explore uncharted experimental configurations for gravitational wave detectors that could lead to more effective detection strategies, especially given the success of previous designs.
AI.method: Utilizing artificial intelligence to systematically explore a wide space of potential detector designs, revealing new configurations that outperform existing designs.
AI.result: More than 50 superior gravitational wave detector designs have been identified, which are shared in a publicly accessible collection, showcasing their effectiveness across various astrophysical contexts.
AI.conclusion: The use of AI in this research not only enhances gravitational wave detection methods but also serves as a foundation for applying AI in experimental design across various fields of fundamental physics.
